review_theme: Floating balloon: force versus initial acceleration
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: A rising balloon is consistent with F_B>W and net upward acceleration if drag/other forces do not negate it. Pressure and displaced air volume can vary during ascent.

review_theme: Cargo loading and safe floating equilibrium
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: More cargo requires more displaced sea water weight for a new stable float; the vessel must still have enough hull reserve, freeboard and stability.

A model boat can sink after overload because total weight exceeds buoyancy it can develop without flooding or losing stable flotation; simply adding weight does not instantly remove hydrostatic pressure.
Placing ballast lower can improve a ship's righting stability in a specified hull/loading configuration but cannot alone guarantee seaworthiness, freeboard or full stability.
Taking water into ballast tanks increases total mass; for approximately unchanged external displaced hull volume, weight can exceed upthrust and cause downward acceleration.

review_theme: Neutral buoyancy is equilibrium under force assumptions
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: F_B=W gives zero vertical net force ONLY when there are no other vertical thrust/support/drag forces. A motionless submarine at depth is consistent with that two-force model; equal forces do not alone prove zero velocity.
Expelling seawater with compressed air lowers total mass while outer displacement is approximately unchanged, enabling upward net force; extra propulsion or drag may affect actual movement.

review_theme: Water-filled mug open versus sealed geometry
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: QUESTION AMBIGUITY: an open water-filled mug lifted out while retaining water has a different water-load and pressure balance from a sealed hollow vessel, whereas an open mug that drains loses internal water. The sole source-best answer D invokes lost water buoyancy but the extent and composition of apparent weight change depend on retention, geometry and support. Specify mug orientation and whether contents stay; do not use as certified exam item without teacher wording decision.
Selection of components capable of carrying vibration and loads primarily addresses structural reliability; buoyancy and stability remain separate design requirements.

review_theme: Stability versus buoyancy and unverified original attribution
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: Adequate buoyancy alone does not ensure righting stability when high mass placement raises the centre of gravity. The source explanation's claim that original textbook specifically emphasizes low loads has not been verified against printed NBF pp.89–91.

review_theme: Equal upthrust for equal fully immersed displaced volumes
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: Wood and iron cubes of equal external volume each fully submerged in the same uniform-density water at the same g have equal F_B; the wood cube may have to be held submerged.

review_theme: Total ship mass and displaced water
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: The hollow vessel has large possible displacement relative to ship plus cargo weight; compact solid steel still receives upthrust, just insufficient to balance its weight.
A completely immersed rigid body of fixed displaced volume in an effectively uniform-density incompressible liquid experiences unchanged ideal F_B as absolute depth increases.
For identical rigid fully submerged objects of equal displaced volumes at comparable g, F_B=ρ_fluid gV is higher in the denser liquid; do not generalize to freely floating bodies.

review_theme: Maximum potential displacement versus equilibrium displacement
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: A hull redesign permitting more possible displacement improves potential load-carrying buoyant support. At unchanged ship total weight, its ACTUAL equilibrium displaced-water weight stays the same, so the source answer must not be explained as necessarily greater current buoyancy.

review_theme: Net upward force is acceleration not guaranteed upward motion
scientific_and_teacher_review_note: 55 N up minus 40 N down = 15 N net upward only if no other vertical forces. This yields UPWARD ACCELERATION; an object initially moving downward may still be descending at that moment. 'Tends to rise' needs clear interpretation.
